paper_title: Detecting Arbitrary Planted Subgraphs in Random Graphs
statement: 1. Closing the gaps between our statistical lower and upper bounds in the sparse and critical regimes (i.e., Theorems 6 and 7) remains an important and challenging problem. We conjecture that the lower bound is the looser part, requiring more sophisticated combinatorial estimates (as in Lemma 24) and decomposition arguments.
context: 5. Outlook We hope our work has opened more doors than it closes. We conclude the paper with a few open problems and exciting directions for future work: 1. Closing the gaps between our statistical lower and upper bounds in the sparse and critical regimes (i.e., Theorems 6 and 7) remains an important and challenging problem. We conjecture that the lower bound is the looser part, requiring more sophisticated combinatorial estimates (as in Lemma 24) and decomposition arguments. 2. Providing additional evidence for the statistical-computational gaps we conjecture using the LDP framework is quite interesting—for example, through average-case reductions (see, for example, Brennan et al. (2018)). 3. Devising robust detection algorithms is of particular interest. One promising approach is to study semirandom models, where an adversary can modify the observed graph—for example, by arbitrarily adding/removing edges while preserving the planted subgraph. Although this has been studied for cliques in Feige and Krauthgamer (2000); Feige and Kilian (2001); Buhai et al. (2023); Błasiok et al. (2024), it remains widely open for other planted subgraphs.

Studying query models, where only a small part of the graph can be investigated—such as the one in Huleihel et al. (2024) for cliques, but in the context of general planted subgraphs—is of practical importance.
